messages.text: is CI red? if so, fix it
Yes, lots of red. Let me get the failing jobs.
Detached HEAD is an ancestor of origin/master, so I'll fast-forward to it and then dispatch diagnosis in parallel.
Pushed the push-CI fix (`910db25f5`). Now dispatching fixes for the scheduled-CI failures (jemalloc notice, Windows portability) and a diagnosis of the Apple/Windows Rust resolution failures.
The diffs look reasonable. Committing the two groups separately.
Pushed. Dave's PR #3742 (policy smoke) also landed. Remaining: the ~100 scheduled-only Rust failures, which Linux has never actually run. Sending a child to reproduce them on Linux.
The child's sandbox saw the mbx cache as read-only; it is writable from my shell. I'll run the scheduled-only tests on Linux myself, since the child could not.
I'm waiting for the Linux run of the 94 scheduled-only tests to finish. I'll continue as soon as it reports.
Children in this session now run in a sandbox that can't write to the mbx cache or reach GitHub, so I'll do this investigation myself.
I'm finding which commit broke the 93 scheduled Rust tests: the nightly run passed on Sep 27 and failed on Sep 28.
I'm checking whether the Rust resolver failures already belong to the in-progress migration epic before deciding to fix them here.

Yes, CI was red. Push CI is now green, but two things are still red that I did not fix. Both need a decision from you.

**Now green**
- **Push CI:** the latest master runs (`88bb4a3a8`, `b0144c0fc`) pass. The failure was `code_query_tutorials::receiver_traversal_tutorial`. Commit `42985a003` added statement entries to JS/TS lowering, so `scope_nodes` went from 1938 to 1952. The receiver result itself did not change, so I updated the number in the tutorial doc (`910db25f5`).
- **policy-scan-smoke:** Dave's PR #3742 fixed this, and it now passes.

**Fixed, waiting for the next scheduled run**
- `50237febe`: the nightly license step failed because `tikv-jemalloc-sys` was not in the audited native-link list. Commit `9ace0fd9d` made jemalloc the allocator. I added its BSD-2-Clause notice and regenerated the notices file. The local license checks pass.
- `73c507a47` fixes three Windows-only problems:
  - Two tests broke on Windows line endings (CRLF).
  - Four tests used Unix-style fixture roots, which are not absolute paths on Windows.
  - C++ include resolution failed for absolute include paths on Windows. It now compares `Path` components instead of converted strings.
  
  These tests pass on Linux. I could not run Windows, so the fix is not confirmed there.

**Still red: needs your decision**

1. **93 Rust resolver tests fail in Hourly and Nightly CI.** They looked like macOS and Windows failures only because the Linux jobs never got to the test step. They also fail on Linux: 93 of 94 in my run (`/tmp/sched-linux.log`).
   - These tests only compile under `--cfg scheduled_tests`, and push CI does not set that flag. That is how the regressions got through.
   - They are real behavior changes, not stale tests. For example, `Self::START_FIELD` now resolves as ambiguous between the associated constant and the module constant.
   - Nightly passed at `0796cb72c` (Sep 27) and has failed since. The Rust move onto the new #2771 resolution system landed that day. That timing points to it as the likely cause, but I have not confirmed it.
   - This is large resolver work, and epic #3726 treats Rust as its regression control. I stopped here so I don't conflict with whoever owns that epic.
   - I recommend opening a P0 CI issue with the test list and log, assigned to the #3726 owners. The policy CLI test in the same set is already tracked in #3421.
2. **The "Release analyzer validation" gate** compares performance against a fixed baseline commit. It has three separate problems:
   - Some runs hit the 120 s measurement timeout (`scripts/quick-performance-signal.py:57`). Raising it to 180 s would help.
   - One run showed a new slow case, `gin-go/query_code/exact-engine-type/mcp`: the first (cold) query went from 53 ms to 109 ms. That may be noise near the 50 ms threshold.
   - The gate rejects runs where a known slow case gives an unclear result.
   
   Whether to raise the timeout, run more samples, or add the new case to the exceptions is a performance-policy choice. I did not change anything.

Do you want me to open the issue for item 1, raise the timeout for item 2, or start fixing the Rust regressions myself?
hitting 120s timeout means "we already know it's too slow" right?
I'm checking how long the benchmark blocks take in passing runs versus timed-out ones.

Mostly yes. The block durations back that up, with one caveat about what the timeout measures.

**What the 120 s limit covers:** one whole benchmark block. That is one run of `bifrost_benchmark run` over every scenario in the manifest (`scripts/quick-performance-signal.py:1144`). It is not a per-scenario threshold.

**What the runs show** (`measurement_seconds` in each run's `summary.md`):

| Run | Baseline block | Candidate block | Result |
|---|---|---|---|
| 36556192462 (green) | 11.9–12.4 s | 101.9–103.1 s | pass |
| 36553561845 (green) | 12.7 s | 104.8–105.3 s | pass |
| 36571126391 | 13.5–14.1 s | 115.5–116.7 s | complete, failed comparison |
| 36529244129 | 14.2–14.9 s | 118.9–119.3 s, then one hit 120 s | timeout |
| 36567898112 | 16.4 s | hit 120 s | timeout |

What this shows:
- The current build takes about 8 times as long as the baseline commit on the same scenarios, in every run. That is already known. The complete runs pass only because the slow scenarios (mostly the workspace builds) are on the approved exception list.
- In runs that timed out, the baseline block was also slower, by about 20–35% (14.2–16.4 s instead of 12 s). That suggests a slower runner, not a slower build. A candidate that normally needs about 105 s then goes past 120 s.

So a timeout adds no new information. It is the known slowdown plus a slow runner. Raising the limit to 180 s would turn these runs into complete comparisons, which would most likely pass under the existing exceptions. That hides nothing new, but it also does not make the build any faster.

One thing I don't know: whether the approved exceptions explain the whole 8x, or whether the time not covered by an exception has been growing. The candidate blocks crept from about 102 s to about 116 s across these runs, but the baseline blocks moved too, so I can't separate build changes from runner speed. Breaking down each candidate block's time by scenario would answer that.
